ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating Learned Static Feature Biases in Temporal Vision-Language Models
PROPOSAL: Analyze a set of pre-trained temporal vision-language models (VLMs) using a novel synthetic dataset GenerationForStaticBiasTemporalData, which combines images with generated sequential scenarios that isolate the effect of static features (e.g., objects in the scene, colors) on model performance. The dataset will feature multiple image sequences, each with a specific static feature (e.g., presence of a tree, color of the object).
CONTROLS: Compare with a baseline model that uses random features as input, and ablate the effect of using pre-trained VLMs by training a new model from scratch on the same dataset.
COST: 30,000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to identify certain static features that consistently reduce the performance of the VLMs on the predicted task, when hidden in the image sequence. We suspect models tend to rely more on certain colors or objects than others. Likely failure points will be models designed to identify high-level activities in video.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Bias Attribution for Temporal Vision-Language Models
PROPOSAL: Propose a novel bias attribution method, TA-Seg, which focuses on identifying the segments within a sequence where the static features have a significant impact on the model's predictions. TA-Seg monitors the model's predictions at each time step and calculates the feature's contribution to the prediction error when the feature is removed from the input.
CONTROLS: Compare TA-Seg with existing bias attribution methods like GradCAM, and ablate the impact of using TA-Seg on the model's performance.
COST: 10,000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect TA-Seg to correctly identify the time points within a sequence where the static features are most influential. However, this method might fail on VLMs that have extremely complex prediction mechanisms or when dealing with highly dynamic scenes where the static features are hard to differentiate from the moving parts.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Investigating Learned Static Feature Biases in Temporal Vision-Language Models
PROPOSAL: REPEAT the analysis of pre-trained temporal VLMs using the GenerationForStaticBiasTemporalData, but this time include a controlled evaluation of the proposed bias attribution method, TA-Seg, from Turn 2. By using the synthetically controlled scenario, we will evaluate the bias attribution's accuracy in identifying error-inducing static features, and compare it to other attribution methods like GradCAM.
CONTROLS: Include a comparison with TA-Seg as well as the baseline of random features, also keep the ablation study for training a VLM from scratch.
COST: 10,000 GPU-hours (new demand added for evaluation of TA-Seg)
PREDICTION: This revised analysis will allow us to not only identify promising biases but also evaluate the potential of bias attribution techniques for accurate identification. However, it may still struggle with models that incorporate too complex a decision-making process or dealing with tough segment detection. Additionally we need to calculate the automation on this task by scenario incorporating some forms of occlusion or noise.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Investigating Learned Static Feature Biases in Temporal Vision-Language Models
PROPOSAL: Incorporate a new analysis on the healthcare-related task of Chest X-ray pneumonia progression classification, using a synthetic dataset that includes both static features (e.g., density of the lungs, presence of certain structures) and temporal features (e.g., changes in lung density, progression of the pneumonia). Evaluate whether the identified static features are relevant to the progression of pneumonia, and compare this with the static features identified in the human activity recognition in video.
CONTROLS: Only include VLMs with prior experience in medical imaging tasks, and compare with the pre-experiment with random baseline and a method with weight .
COST: 20,000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect some overlap in the error-inducing static features identified across the two tasks, showcasing the generalizability of these biases. However, the performance may degrade due to model variations in interpretability.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Label-Agnostic Static Bias Detection
PROPOSAL: Propose a new approach, Label-Agnostic Static Bias Detection (LABD), which identifies static features without relying on task-specific labels. LABD uses a multi-task learning scheme where the VLM is trained to perform multiple tasks simultaneously, such as both human activity recognition and sentiment analysis on the same image sequence. The goal is to see if static biases survive when model learns to 'intrinsically care' and can then help detect the intrinsic biases under normal conditions .
CONTROLS: Compare LABD with the proposed TA-Seg and existing bias attribution methods on a variety of tasks, including the ones covered in previous proposals.
COST: 30,000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect LABD to capture more general, ubiquitous static biases, but its performance might be reduced due to the increased complexity of training multiple tasks simultaneously. Model choice should also optimize for the desired specific goals rather than fine-tuning to interface well and differentiate the bias thru regularization considerations.

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: Label-Agnostic Static Bias Detection
PROPOSAL: MODULATE the multi-task learning approach in LABD by incorporating a novel regularizer that encourages the VLM to focus on the structural features of the image sequence, such as edges and textures, rather than task-specific features. This will help to identify static biases that are robust to changes in the task or labels.
CONTROLS: Compare the modified LABD with the original LABD, TA-Seg, and other bias attribution methods on the same set of tasks and datasets.
COST: 5,000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect the modified LABD to improve the identification of static biases and provide a more robust and generalizable approach. However, this might come at the cost of decreased performance on specific tasks, and handling the risk that detection of bias via over regularized and heavily narrow non-specific will allow transmodel inference.

CONTROLS: Compare the incorporation of domain knowledge with the previous proposals on the same set of tasks and datasets.
COST: 20,000 GPU-hours

Can make fake successes in validity of identified fixed errors, reducing algorithm stability.

This will leverage the strengths of both approaches and provide a more robust and accurate method for identifying static biases.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Active Learning for Static Bias Detection
PROPOSAL: Introduce an active learning framework that iteratively selects the most informative instances from the data to be labeled by human experts, with the goal of identifying the most error-inducing static biases. The framework will use a combination of uncertainty sampling and sensitivity analysis to select the most informative instances.
CONTROLS: Compare the active learning framework with the previous proposals on the same set of tasks and datasets, and evaluate its performance in terms of efficiency and accuracy.
COST: 40,000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect the active learning framework to improve the efficiency of static bias detection by reducing the number of instances that need to be labeled by human experts. However, this approach may be computationally expensive and may require careful tuning of the hyperparameters to achieve optimal performance. Also, dependency on manpower for confirmation in place might hinder adaptability.

TITLE: Scalable and Explainable Static Bias Detection Framework
PROPOSAL: Combine the insights from the previous proposals to develop a scalable and explainable framework for static bias detection. The framework will integrate the bias attribution models, domain knowledge, and active learning to provide a comprehensive understanding of the error-inducing static biases. The framework will be designed to be explainable, allowing users to understand the reasons behind the identified biases.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the framework on a large-scale dataset and compare its performance with state-of-the-art methods.
COST: 100,000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect the framework to provide a comprehensive understanding of the error-inducing static biases and improve the accuracy and explainability of static bias detection. However, this approach may be computationally expensive and may require careful tuning of the hyperparameters to achieve optimal performance. Also, ensuring the explainability of the framework may be challenging.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Automated Detection of Error-Inducing Static Features in Temporal VLMs
PROPOSAL: Investigate the use of statistical hypothesis testing to identify static features that are significantly correlated with model prediction errors on a validation set. Utilize a linear Mixed-Effects Model (LMM) with random effects for both images and features to account for temporal dependencies and potential correlations between features. Use a method such as permutation-based hypothesis testing to assess significance and identify the threshold above which a feature is considered error-inducing. Given that the true biases of trained models are generally unknown, evaluate the accuracy of this approach by comparing the extracted biases to those found through manual analysis on a subset of the validation set.
CONTROLS: Compare to existing methods such as GradCAM, and ablate the LMM by reducing the number of random effects.
COST: 30 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This approach will reveal some error-inducing static features, but may struggle to identify those that are correlated with specific class labels rather than overall prediction errors.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Feature Importance through Conditional Sampling
PROPOSAL: Develop a method to quantify the importance of each feature by selectively removing them from the input sequence and measuring the change in model predictions. This can be achieved by introducing a conditional sampling mechanism where a fraction of the images in the sequence are replaced with random images that mask the feature in question. Measure the drop in accuracy when this feature is removed and compare it to a baseline where the removed images are replaced with the original ones. This approach will allow for feature-level attribution and can help identify error-inducing features that are critical for the model's decision-making process.
CONTROLS: Compare to the LMM approach (proposal 1) to see if feature importance is more interpretable, and ablate by varying the fraction of removed images.
COST: 40 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This approach may be computationally expensive due to the need to sample multiple conditional sequences, but it can provide more fine-grained insights into how each feature contributes to the model's predictions.

ACTION: REVISE 1
REASON: Add a layer of interpretation to the linear Mixed-Effects Model (LMM) to make the extracted feature correlations more interpretable.
PROPOSAL (Revise 1): Reconsider the LMM (Automated Detection of Error-Inducing Static Features in Temporal VLMs) by replacing the feature unit codes with interpretability-focused feature relevance scores (e.g. SHAP or LIME). Use permutation-based hypothesis testing to assess significance while accounting for the relevance scores, thereby obtaining a relationship matrix that can detect error-inducing static features and explicitly tell which subset of features is strongly influencing the model's predictions. Given that the true biases of trained models are generally unknown, evaluate the accuracy of this revised approach by comparing the extracted biases to those found through manual analysis on a subset of the validation set.
CONTROLS: Include comparisons to proposal 2, and ablate the LMM to reduce the effect of relevance scores on the permutation-based hypothesis testing.
COST: 35 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The addition of feature relevance information is expected to improve the model's ability to identify truly error-inducing static features, albeit at increased computational cost.

TITLE: Temporal Attention Pattern Analysis
PROPOSAL: Investigate the use of attention mechanisms within the temporal VLM to identify salient regions of the input sequence that contribute to the model's errors. Analyze the attention weights across different features and frames to identify attention patterns that are significantly correlated with error-inducing static features. Utilize permutation-based hypothesis testing to assess the significance of these patterns and refine the results by considering granular feature-level attention weights. Given that the true biases of trained models are generally unknown, evaluate the accuracy of this approach by comparing the extracted biases to those found through manual analysis on a subset of the validation set.
CONTROLS: Compare to existing methods such as GradCAM and ablate the attention mechanism to verify its effectiveness.
COST: 50 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This approach may reveal nuanced attention patterns that correspond to error-inducing static features, but may require manual interpretation of the attention weights to fully understand their significance.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Gradient-Based Feature Importance Analysis
PROPOSAL: Adapt a gradient-based attribution method, such as the Residual Analysis (RA) or the Integrated Gradients (IG), to quantify the contribution of each feature to the model's predictions across the input sequence. By analyzing the gradients of the model's output with respect to its input, identify features that have a significant and large impact on the prediction, hinting at potential error-inducing static features. To account for temporal dependencies, slice the input sequence into multiple chunks and calculate feature importance within each chunk, allowing the method to capture correlation structures between features.
CONTROLS: Compare to existing feature importance methods (e.g. feature attribution through the LMM, conditional sampling), and ablate the temporal chunking approach to understand its effect on gradient similarity.
COST: 45 GPU-hours
PREDICION: Gradient-based methods might require careful data scaling and normalization to avoid feature dominance, but they provide a way to quantify the specific contribution of static features to a model's predictions.

TITLE: Synthetic Data Generation for Bias Detection
PROPOSAL: Develop a model-agnostic data generation framework to create synthetic sequences that perturb specific static features while keeping the rest of the input fixed. Use these synthetic sequences to test the robustness of the temporal VLM and the effectiveness of the existing methods in detecting error-inducing static features. Generate a diverse set of synthetic sequences by varying the types and levels of feature perturbations, allowing for a comprehensive evaluation of the methods' limitations and potential biases. Evaluate the performance of existing methods on the generated data and compare it to their performance on the original validation set.
CONTROLS: Include a comparison to the performance of existing methods on real-world data, and ablate the size and diversity of the synthetic dataset to understand their effect on evaluation results.
COST: 20 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Synthetic data generation will allow for the assessment of the robustness of the existing methods in a controlled environment, potentially revealing their limitations and biases, but may introduce new challenges in terms of data quality and realism.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Transfer Learning from Phenomenon-Agnostic Bias Detection
PROPOSAL: Train a transfer learning model on datasets and tasks from different domains that are known to suffer from similar types of biases (e.g., image recognition, natural language processing, or other vision-language tasks not related to temporal VLMs). Use this pre-trained model as a starting point to adapt it to the specific task of bias detection for temporal VLMs. Fine-tune the model on a set of features that have been identified as potential error-inducing static features and evaluate its performance on new unseen features. This approach leverages the knowledge from other tasks and domains to enhance the detection of biases in temporal VLMs.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the transferability of the pre-trained model across different vision-language tasks, and compare its performance with the existing methods proposed in this research.
COST: 60 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Transfer learning may improve the detection of biases in temporal VLMs by leveraging the expertise learned from similar biases in other tasks, but its effectiveness depends heavily on the quality of the pre-trained model and the adaptation process.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Model Auditing with Data Augmentation
PROPOSAL: Develop a data augmentation-based framework to analyze the sensitivity of the temporal VLM to specific static features by augmenting the input sequences with perturbed static features. Use a robustness-inspired data augmentation strategy to perturb the static features in a way that resembles real-world variations. Evaluate the model's performance on the augmented data to understand its sensitivity to different types of static features and identify those that have a significant impact on the model's predictions. This approach can provide insights into the model's flaws and help developers understand how to address them.
CONTROLS: Compare to other model-agnostic bias detection methods, and evaluate the sensitivity of different types of temporal VLMs to various augmented features.
COST: 35 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Model auditing with data augmentation can reveal the model's vulnerabilities to specific static features, but may require a large amount of computational resources to generate and evaluate the augmented data.

proposal: In this approach, we will utilize t-distributed Stochastic Neighbor Embedding (t-SNE) to reduce the dimensionality of the feature space of the temporal VLM's output for a given sequence. By visualizing the embeddings using t-SNE, we can identify clusters or groups of data points (corresponding to different static feature distributions) within the feature space. This technique is often used for visualizing high-dimensional data and identifying patterns, such as dense regions or communities, in low-dimensional space.

title: reducing static feature biases in temporal vlms with data augmentation
proposal: This work explores the use of data augmentation as a means to reduce static feature biases in temporal VLMs. We will train the models on augmented datasets that intentionally include a wider variety of static features or their absence, forcing the model to learn features that are invariant to these changes. This could potentially reduce the reliance on static feature biases learned by the model. We will implement additional augmentations tailored for temporal data, such as time-warps, flipping, and resizing sequences, as well as applying random noise to the images. We evaluate this approach on a benchmark of synthetic video datasets.
controls: We compare the results from the augmented training with a baseline model trained on the original dataset and test how these methods reduce biases on class distributions outside that baseline.

prediction: Empirical results will show that our proposed method significantly improves the performance of the VLM in terms of reduced biases, yet the preservation of applicability for understanding temporal sequential aspects may take some adaptation.

proposal: We combine the previous methods to evaluate the performance and effectiveness of different approaches for identifying and mitigating static feature biases in temporal VLMs. We will apply both individual methods (e.g. logit analysis and decision boundary analysis) and ensemble methods (e.g. combining the results of multiple methods) to a suite of benchmark datasets, including synthetic and real-world data in human activity recognition and chest X-ray pneumonia progression classification.
